chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Abu al-Khattab, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Habib al-Kha'thami, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) commanded that circumambulation be performed on behalf of the one with a distended belly and the one with a broken bone.

And what we mentioned regarding that those with this description are expected to be healed; if they heal, [they perform it themselves], and if not, circumambulation is performed on their behalf; this has been narrated.
78 - Musa ibn al-Qasim, from Abu Ja'far Muhammad al-Ahmasi, from Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Bajali, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) or wrote to him - from Sa'id ibn Yasar - that he fell from his camel and his belly does not hold together [is distended]; do I circumambulate on his behalf and run [in Sa'i]? He said: 'No, but leave him; if he heals, he will perform it himself, and if not, you perform it on his behalf.'

key_terms.الْكَسِيرِ: The one with a broken bone
key_terms.الْمَبْطُونِ: The one with a distended belly
key_terms.طِيفَ عَنْهُ: Circumambulation is performed on his behalf

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for performing Hajj rituals on behalf of someone who is too ill to perform them themselves?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the juristic distinction between *Tawaf al-Ada'* (obligatory performance) and *Tawaf al-Nafl* (voluntary), establishing that the sick person retains the primary obligation to perform it personally upon recovery. The ruling reflects the Shia principle that acts of worship requiring physical capability are deferred rather than substituted, unless the incapacity becomes permanent or the person passes away, in which case a proxy performs it. This highlights the scholarly emphasis on preserving the individual's direct connection to the ritual when possible.
